Welsh is a Celtic language spoken primarily in Wales and the only surviving Celtic language with a continuous literary tradition stretching back to the sixth century. It is a Brythonic Celtic language, more distantly related to Irish and Scottish Gaelic than to other European languages. Welsh is the language of Welsh mythology and early medieval Welsh poetry including the Mabinogion and works by the poets Aneirin and Taliesin, and it possesses the oldest substantial literature of any Celtic language. Today roughly 870,000 people speak Welsh, with about 750,000 claiming some competence in the language, with native speakers concentrated in the North and West Wales. The language features a complex system of initial consonant mutation, which involves sound changes at the start of words based on grammatical context, a defining feature shared with Irish and Breton but unique among modern European languages. A written standard was established in the early twentieth century. Welsh place names, legal status, and media presence, particularly through S4C the Welsh-language television channel, reflect modern language policy initiatives aimed at protection and revival. Despite centuries of English political dominance, Welsh has persisted and undergone a twentieth and twenty-first century revival, and it stands as an exemplar of deliberate language preservation through education and media policy. It remains the most viable Celtic language, with the largest speaker base and most robust institutional support.
